text_to_speech: The accelerator is almost like a family member and this is like a family home. I'm Mahananda Dasgupta and I work at the Heavy Ion Accelerator Facility at the ANU . It is where I do all my research. So this is the control room of the accelerators. We can monitor all the parameters of the accelerator and we can control each of the 600 plus elements of the accelerator sitting here. The Heavy Ion Accelerator Facility is coming up to be 50 years old. It is one of three highest energy ion accelerators of this type in the world. It accelerates particles to very high velocities. So it can go up to, for example, protons up to 30,000 kilometres per second. And what does that do? What essentially it does is it is like an extremely sharp stick with which you can poke the heart of the atom, which is the nucleus. You can see what it does. You can bring two nuclei together. Well I stare at this place more often than I stare at the back of my hand. It is not just a scientific investment. It is somehow an emotional connection to a piece of infrastructure which has given me personally a lot in order to make scientific advances. If you are using the other accelerator that comes along, gets accelerated over in that arm, goes around and then gets sent here. Why is this tortuous path? Because we didn't have enough space to put the accelerator. This lab is an integral part of my being. I'm deeply connected to the lab. Much more than I'm connected to my home. So all along the path that you will see, there are instruments to control the beam of particles, make it the shape we desire, and move it in X and Y direction and monitor it at all times. As a tower for us, it is a tower of strength because it has stood there for the last 50 years, pushing out, helping us push out great science together with the technical staff and the academic ideas, we are able to innovate. It's an Australian triumph, I would say.
